To leave, especially a building.

examples.text: Please go out through the back door.

glosses: To leave one's abode to go to public places, especially for recreation or entertainment.

examples.text: They were going to stay in and read, but instead went out shopping.
On their first date they went out to dinner at a restaurant.
Let's go out tonight and have some fun!
A ſower went out to ſowe his ſeede / and as he ſowed / ſome fell by the waye ſyde / and hit was troden vnder fete / and the foules of the ayre devoured it vp.
It seems like we go out for pizza a lot these days.

glosses: To be eliminated from a competition.

examples.text: Our team went out in the third round.

glosses: To come to an end, by nature or by an unseen external agent.
To be turned off or extinguished.

examples.text: The lights went out while I was taking a shower.

glosses: To come to an end, by nature or by an unseen external agent.
To go unconscious; to pass out.

examples.text: When I hit him, he hit the floor and went out.

glosses: To come to an end, by nature or by an unseen external agent.
To be drained from; to disappear from somebody.

examples.text: All the fizz has already gone out of the election campaign.
After diagnosis, all his confidence went out of him.

glosses: To come to an end, by nature or by an unseen external agent.
To become extinct, to expire.

examples.text: And cold the poor man lies at night, / And so goes out the year.

glosses: To come to an end, by nature or by an unseen external agent.
To die.

examples.text: As much as you may want to plan your funeral, you can't control when you go out.

1977-1980, Lou Sullivan, personal diary, quoted in 2019, Ellis Martin, Zach Ozma (editors), We Both Laughed In Pleasure
A motorcycle cop led the funeral procession & with all the cabs pulling up the rear we were 5–6 blocks long. The cops even blocked off streets for us. The guy went out like a goddamn mayor.

glosses: To discard or meld all the cards in one's hand.

examples.text: Leon made two canastas, then went out by melding treys.

glosses: To pass out of fashion.

examples.text: He thought Nehru jackets went out in the late seventies.
And ‘blubbing’ . . . Blubbing went out with ‘decent’ and ‘ripping’. Mind you, not a bad new language to start up. 1920s schoolboy slang could be due for a revival.

glosses: To have a romantic relationship, one that involves going out together on dates; to be a couple.

examples.text: They've been going out for three years now, but still live apart.
Jack and Susan are going out.

glosses: To have a romantic relationship (with someone).

examples.text: Do you think she will go out with anyone this year?

glosses: To fail.

examples.text: I'd like to help clear the field, but my knee went out on me.

glosses: To spend the last moments of a show (while playing something).

examples.text: Thank you for introducing us to your new album. Which song should we go out on?

glosses: To recede; to ebb.
To sympathize with; to express positive feelings towards.

examples.text: Our thoughts and prayers go out to those afflicted by the tragedy.
My heart went out to her, but there was nothing I could do.

glosses: To take part in a duel (with).

examples.text: He went out at the firſt hint with the Neapolitan, and being an admirable ſwordſman, wounded and diſarmed him; […]
He must go out or be under a social ban. Out they go accordingly, and the trained pistol-shot kills his civilian opponent.

glosses: To be broadcast.

examples.text: The first episode of the show goes out on Saturday.
